L27: Spectral anomaly detection in hyperspectral imagery is concerned with identifying unusual spectra that occur infrequently within the image. The model applied in this paper is based on the idea that background pixels reside on, or near, lower dimensional manifolds (surfaces) in the higher-dimensional spectral space. Using a similarity graph to approximate the theoretical background manifold(s), we investigate how edge-weighting functions influence the detection of anomalous spectra.
L28: The edge-weighting functions used here include the reciprocal Euclidean distance and the heat kernel with varying parameters. The data are then transformed into a vector space that preserves graph structure and the Reed-Xiaoli (RX) anomaly detection algorithm is applied to expose anomalies.

L106: 1. INTRODUCTION
L107: 
L108: The objective of spectral anomaly detection in hyper-
L109: 
L110: spectral imagery is to identify unusual spectra that oc-
L111: 
L112: cur infrequently within the image. The problem for-
L113: 
L114: mulation is very similar to target detection, but it dif-
L115: 
L116: fers in one major aspect: no a priori information exists
L117: to indicate how anomalous spectra manifest in spectral
L118: 
L119: space,i.e., the vector space with each axis corresponding
L120: 
L121: to a spectral band of the image. To expose anomalous
L122: 
L123: spectra, a mathematical model is applied to capture the
L124: 
L125: background structure of the data, and spectra that de-
L126: 
L127: viate from this model are labeled as anomalies. For
L128: 
L129: example, the global implementation of the Reed-Xiaoli
L130: 
L131: (RX) algorithm models the data with a multivariate nor-
L132: 
L133: mal density, and the squared Mahalanobis distance of
L134: each pixel from the mean vector provides a measure of
L135: 
L136: how di ﬀ erent it is from the background[1].
L137: 
L138: The model applied here is based on the assump-
L139: 
L140: tion that all in-scene pixels reside on, or near, lower-
L141: 
L142: dimensional manifolds (surfaces) in spectral space. In

L153:

L155: to capture the intricate structure of these manifolds, we
L156:

L159: model. Graph-based models have become increasingly
L160: 
L161: popular in hyperspectral image analysis in recent years

L163: and have found application in classiﬁcation[2, 3, 4],
L164: 
L165: anomaly detection[5, 6], and change detection. As re-
L166: 
L167: viewed in the following section, a graph consists of
L168: 
L169: vertices, edges, and an edge-weighting function that
L170: 
L171: provides a measure of similarity between the endpoints
L172: of an edge. In the context of hyperspectral imagery,
L173: 
L174: the pixels become the vertices in the graph and edges
L175: 
L176: connect pixels that are spectrally similar. This paper in-
L177: 
L178: vestigates how changes in the edge-weighting function
L179: 
L180: inﬂuence the detection of spectral anomalies.

L182: This paper is organized in the following manner. Sec-

L189: tral data set used and the experimental results obtained.

L193: 2. METHODOLOGY
L194: 
L195: An undirected weighted graph G=(V,E, ω) is com-
L196: 
L197: posed of two ﬁnite sets, called the vertex set V and edge
L198: 
L199: set E, as well as the edge-weighting function ω that as-
L200: 
L201: signs a positive value to each edge in E. The magnitude
L202: 
L203: of the weight corresponds to the amount of similarity
L204: 
L205: between the endpoints of the edge. When two vertices
L206: 
L207: are connected by an edge, they are said to be adjacent
L208: and the adjacency structure of G can be represented by
L209: 
L210: a matrix, called the weighted adjacency matrix W. Given a
L211: 
L212: graph with N vertices, W is an N×N matrix whose rows
L213: 
L214: and columns correspond to an arbitrary ordering of the
L215: 
L216: vertices; its nonzero entries correspond to the weights
L217: 
L218: assigned to the edges connecting them. That is, if an
L219: 
L220: edge exists between vertices v i and v j, then [W]ij =ω ij .
L221: 
L222: By convention, if vertices v i and v j are not adjacent, then
L223: [W]ij =0. The weighted degree of a vertex v i, denoted as
L224: 
L225: deg(v i), is the sum of the weighted edges that connect to
L226: 
L227: it. The weighted degree matrix D is an N×N diagonal
L228: 
L229: matrix with [D]ii =deg(v i). The graph Laplacian L is

L476: 4. SUMMARY
L477: 
L478: When applying an undirected weighted graphical
L479: 
L480: model to hyperspectral data, it is important to con-
L481: 
L482: sider the edge-weighing function used. In this paper,
L483: we applied two functions and analyzed their e ﬀ ects on
L484: 
L485: exposing spectral anomalies. As discussed in Section
L486: 
L487: 3, using a function with an appropriate rate of decrease
L488: 
L489: helps to expose anomalies in the data set. However,
L490: 
L491: as also demonstrated, using a function that approaches
L492: 
L493: zero can introduce numerical errors when performing
L494: 
L495: an eigendecomposition on the Laplacian matrix used in
L496: 
L497: the CTD transformation. Furthermore, as we assumed
L498: 
L499: the spectral anomalies in G are the more distant neigh-
L500: bors in E, the weighting function assigns increasingly
L501: 
L502: smaller values to their edges. As the weights assigned to
L503: 
L504: these edges approach zero, the commute time distance
L505: 
L506: approaches inﬁnity. While this may seem favorable
L507: 
L508: for anomaly detection, it dominates the scaling of the
L509: 
L510: embedding and makes weaker anomalies more di ﬃ-
L511: 
L512: cult to detect. In order to avoid these issues, a bias
L513: 
L514:  > 0 was added to the heat kernel function and im-
L515: 
L516: proved results were obtained. This study demonstrates
L517: that one should exercise caution when choosing an
L518: 
L519: edge-weighting function, and the function itself should
L520: 
L521: have the following characteristics: a monotonically de-
L522: 
L523: creasing function with an appropriate rate of decrease,
L524: 
L525: as determined by the nearest neighbor distances, and
L526: 
L527: should approach a constant  > 0 for connected graphs
L528: 
L529: to avoid numerical errors.

Typically, the application involves extracting man-made objects from natural and agricultural surroundings. A large challenge in designing these algorithms is determining which pixels initially constitute the background material within an image.
L643: The topological anomaly detection (TAD) algorithm constructs a graph theory-based, fully non-parametric topological model of the background in the image scene, and uses codensity to measure deviation from this background. In TAD, the initial graph theory structure of the image data is created by connecting an edge between any two pixel vertices x and y if the Euclidean distance between them is less than some resolution r.
L644: While this type of proximity graph is among the most well-known approaches to building a geometric graph based on a given set of data, there is a wide variety of dierent geometrically-based techniques. In this paper, we present a comparative test of the performance of TAD across four dierent constructs of the initial graph: mutual k-nearest neighbor graph, sigma-local graph for two different values of σ > 1, and the proximity graph originally implemented in TAD.

Messinger L657: Spectral image analysis problems often begin by performing a preprocessing step composed of applying a transformation that generates an alternative representation of the spectral data. In this paper, a transformation based on a Markov-chain model of a random walk on a graph is introduced.
L658: More precisely, we quantify the random walk using a quantity known as the average commute time distance and find a nonlinear transformation that embeds the nodes of a graph in a Euclidean space where the separation between them is equal to the square root of this quantity. This has been referred to as the Commute Time Distance (CTD) transformation and it has the important characteristic of increasing when the number of paths between two nodes decreases and/or the lengths of those paths increase.
L659: Remarkably, a closed form solution exists for computing the average commute time distance that avoids running an iterative process and is found by simply performing an eigendecomposition on the graph Laplacian matrix.
L660: Contained in this paper is a discussion of the particular graph constructed on the spectral data for which the commute time distance is then calculated from, an introduction of some important properties of the graph Laplacian matrix, and a subspace projection that approximately preserves the maximal variance of the square root commute time distance.
L661: Finally, RX anomaly detection and Topological Anomaly Detection (TAD) algorithms will be applied to the CTD subspace followed by a discussion of their results.

L672:   * cite25†David Gillis L673:   * cite26†Jeffrey H. Bowles L674: Spectral graph theory has proven to be a useful tool in the analysis of high-dimensional data sets. Recall that, mathematically, a graph is a collection of objects (nodes) and connections between them (edges); a weighted graph additionally assigns numerical values (weights) to the edges. Graphs are represented by their adjacency whose elements are the weights between the nodes.
L675: Spectral graph theory uses the eigendecomposition of the adjacency matrix (or, more generally, the Laplacian of the graph) to derive information about the underlying graph. In this paper, we develop a spectral method based on the 'normalized cuts' algorithm to segment hyperspectral image data (HSI).
L676: In particular, we model an image as a weighted graph whose nodes are the image pixels, and edges defined as connecting spatial neighbors; the edge weights are given by a weighted combination of the spatial and spectral distances between nodes. We then use the Laplacian of the graph to recursively segment the image.
L677: The advantages of our approach are that, first, the graph structure naturally incorporates both the spatial and spectral information present in HSI; also, by using only spatial neighbors, the adjacency matrix is highly sparse; as a result, it is possible to apply our technique to much larger images than previous techniques. In the paper, we present the details of our algorithm, and include experimental results from a variety of hyperspectral images.

Czaja L690:   * cite30†Julia Dobrosotskaya L691:   * cite25†David Gillis L692: We analyze Schroedinger Eigenmaps - a new semi-supervised manifold learning and recovery technique - for applications in hyperspectral imagery. This method is based on an implementation of graph Schroedinger operators with appropriately constructed potentials as carriers of expert/labeled information. In this paper, we analyze the features of Schroedinger Eigenmaps through analysis of the potential locations and their imapct on the classication.
L693: The imaging modalities which we shall incorporate in our analysis include multispectral and hyperspectral imagery. For the purpose of constructing ecient methods for building the potentials we refer to expert ground-truth data, as well as to using automated clustering techniques. We also investigate the role of dierent sources of the barrier potential locations, and the role they play in the separation of classes.
